Alaska plaice (Pleuronectes quadrituberculatus) is a commercially important flatfish inhabiting the continental shelf of the Bering Sea and Gulf of Alaska. Embryonic development proceeds slowly under the cold conditions characteristic of its high-latitude spawning grounds. At a stable incubation temperature of 3.3 °C [T = 3.3 °C], the time from fertilisation to hatching is 49 days [ab = 49 days], a duration that far exceeds the incubation periods of many temperate flatfishes such as Pleuronectes platessa. The newly emerged yolk-sac larva, still reliant on endogenous reserves, has an estimated wet weight at birth of 0.0039 grams [Wwb = 0.0039 grams], reflecting the modest size of the fertilised ovum, which measures between 1.9 and 2.05 mm in diameter. This lecithotrophic phase is critical, as the larva must absorb its yolk mass before the onset of exogenous feeding, a transition that typically occurs within the first several weeks following eclosion.

Growth during the pelagic larval phase proceeds rapidly, though mortality remains high as individuals disperse within the water column. As the teleost larva develops, it undergoes a pronounced larval metamorphosis involving eye migration and a shift from a planktonic to a benthic existence. The size at which 50% of the population attains sexual maturity, or total length at puberty, has been estimated at 30.2 cm [Lp = 30.2 cm], with a reported range of 24 to 37 cm among various survey years. This pubertal milestone corresponds to a wet weight at puberty of approximately 287 grams [Wwp = approximately 287 grams], a value derived from length-weight regressions applied to bottom-trawl survey data collected in the eastern Bering Sea. Individuals below this size threshold are considered immature and are rarely observed in spawning aggregations, suggesting that size, rather than age alone, governs the onset of reproductive activity.

Following settlement, the benthic juvenile enters a prolonged period of somatic growth. Maximum size estimates for Alaska plaice indicate that the ultimate total length can reach 87 cm [Li = 87 cm], a value recorded from historical survey specimens and commercial catches. At this maximal length, the corresponding ultimate wet weight is approximately 7500 grams [Wwi = approximately 7500 grams], as predicted by the species length-weight relationship (a = 0.00794, b ≈ 3.08). The transition from a pre-pubertal juvenile to a spawning adult is marked by a substantial increase in body mass; the mass associated with reproductive activation is estimated at approximately 287 grams [Wwp = approximately 287 grams], whereas fully grown individuals can achieve more than twenty-five times that mass. This dramatic size disparity underscores the energetic demands of reaching asymptotic body size in a cold, seasonally productive ecosystem where food availability fluctuates markedly.

Longevity is a notable feature of the life history of Pleuronectes quadrituberculatus. Under the same cold-water regime typical of its habitat (3.3 °C [T = 3.3 °C]), the maximum lifespan is estimated at approximately 37 years [am = approximately 37 years], a value that makes it one of the longer-lived pleuronectids in the North Pacific. This extended lifespan is consistent with the slow-growth, late-maturing strategy observed in many high-latitude flatfishes. The relationship between temperature and development is evident when comparing the incubation period: the 49-day hatching time (49 days) [ab = 49 days] at 3.3 °C [T = 3.3 °C] is considerably longer than would be expected for a congener spawning in warmer southern waters, illustrating the pronounced effect of thermal regime on early ontogenetic rates in this species.

Reproductive output in Alaska plaice is linked to female body size. A gravid individual measuring near the size at 50% maturity, with a total length of approximately 30.2 cm [Lp = approximately 30.2 cm], typically carries a modest batch of eggs. Fecundity estimates from histological studies indicate that an average female spawns roughly 150,000 eggs per reproductive event, and field observations suggest that most adults produce a single spawning event each year. The combination of a moderate clutch size and an annual spawning frequency results in a relatively low lifetime reproductive output compared to more fecund flatfishes, a pattern that may reflect the energetic constraints imposed by cold temperatures and the slow accumulation of somatic reserves required to achieve the maximum adult mass of 7500 grams [Wwi = 7500 grams]. This iteroparous strategy, paired with a long reproductive lifespan, allows individuals multiple opportunities to contribute to the next generation.
